title: Lift yourself
hook: let a person lift the self by the self; the self is its own friend and enemy (Bhagavad Gita 6.5)
tomorrow: why does a god on a battlefield care how high your seat is?

segments.voice: Yesterday, the full ocean: rivers pour in all day, and the sea stays the sea. In the Gita, desires can flow into a person at peace the same way. The full ocean.

Good news can land like bad news: the offer arrives, suddenly it's real, and the stomach drops. The first chapter of the Bhagavad Gita builds to a man in a far heavier version of that spot. Two armies face each other on the field of Kurukshetra. The conch shells have sounded. Arjuna, the archer, asks his charioteer Krishna to drive him out between the lines, and he looks across: teachers, uncles, cousins, friends. His limbs give way. His mouth goes dry. His bow, Gandiva, slips from his hand. And then he sits down in the chariot and lets the bow and arrows go.
screen: `THE OFFER LANDS. THE STOMACH DROPS.` → `TWO ARMIES, ONE CHARIOT.` → `THE BOW SLIPS.` → `ARJUNA SITS DOWN.`

segments.voice: That's where Arjuna's lesson starts: not with a hero, but with a man who has sat down. Krishna's first answer is sharp: shake off this weakness, and stand. It doesn't work. So the talk goes long, and by the sixth chapter Krishna gives the answer from the inside. Let a person lift the self by the self, and not let the self sink. The self alone is its own friend; the self alone is its own enemy. The next verse turns it: the self is a friend to the one who has mastered it, and an enemy to the one who hasn't. A detail worth passing on: in the Sanskrit, the same word, atman, the self, sits on both sides of the sentence: the one who lifts and the one who's lifted. So in the Gita, being your own friend isn't a pep talk or a mood. It's yoga: a mind trained by its own practice, until the trained part can carry the shaky part. That's why this chapter goes straight on to practice. The Gita doesn't leave everything to effort; later chapters speak of devotion and grace. But this verse is plain. Krishna can drive the chariot and teach. Arjuna has to stand up.
screen: `A MAN WHO HAS SAT DOWN.` · `LIFT THE SELF BY THE SELF.` · `ATMAN ON BOTH SIDES.` · `A FRIEND ONCE TRAINED.` · then, large: `MY OWN FRIEND.`

segments.voice: Find a pen and something to write on. Write one hard thing you're facing, and under it, the sentence the steady, practiced part of you would say about it: not flattery, the true thing. Read it back once, slowly, in your own voice.
Lift yourself: the Gita's line that the self raises the self, and is a friend to the one who has trained it.
Keep this one: my own friend, the part of me that practices. Four days into the Gita.

howItsDone: The Bhagavad Gita is part of the Mahabharata; Hindus study, recite and teach it, and verse 6.5, lift the self by the self, belongs to its chapter on meditation.
